content:
The classification includes over 122 French wines, 17 Italian wines and nine New Zealand wines. Image supplied

Australia’s fine wine authority Langtons has unveiled its inaugural Classification of International Wine, set to “equip fine wine enthusiasts with a relevant and data-driven guide for investment, collection and enjoyment”.

“The inaugural langtons Classification of International Wine indicates a strong and competitive secondary market, with investors shifting their focus on fine wine as not just passion-led play, but as a strategic asset,” said Michael Anderson, Langtons head of auction.

“French wines dominate the Classification of International Wine offering stability and value, but it’s Italy, in particular Piedmont and Tuscany, that’s emerged as a market arbitrage opportunity for forward-thinking investors who are looking to diversify outside of France.”

By expanding its classification globally, Langtons’ objective is to create a definitive guide of “the world’s finest wines where local Australian producers take their rightful place alongside the very best”.

“The wines and producers that make up the Langtons Classification of Australian Wine are of absolute elite status here locally, but it needs to be known more that they sit easily alongside the greats of Burgundy, Bordeaux and Tuscany. Our inaugural Classification of International Wine serves as a powerful benchmarking tool, and we encourage our customers to undertake the comparison themselves to experience the calibre of wine Australian producers are crafting.

“In our classification…we have exceptional examples of Pinot Noir such as the Bass Phillip Reserve, Mount Mary and Bindi Block 5 that are acknowledged with a First Classified status. These wines are easily comparable to the likes of Armand Rousseau, Dujac and Comte Georges de Vogue in the Classification of International Wine and truly hold their own alongside,” said Anderson.

The list features a total of 122 French wines, with Italy holding the second largest share at 17 wines and New Zealand in third place with nine. In terms of varieties, Chardonnay came out on top, a “surprising first place over Bordeaux Cabernet Sauvignon, but a result aligning with the wider shift towards cool-climate, lighter style wines as defined in the Classification of Australian Wine”.

A total of 19 regions feature in the list spanning across France, Italy, New Zealand, the US, Germany, Spain and Portugal. Notable wines include Leroy Musigny, Rayas, Bell Hill Pinot and Chateau D’yquem.

 

‘A shift in investor behaviour’

According to Langtons, there’s a clear movement within investors to see fine wine as not just a lifestyle investment, but as a tangible capital.

“Currently, we’re seeing fi erce competitiveness as multiple bidders vie for the same wines, which drives up prices and encourages more collectors to participate. We utilise a single-vendor strategy for international wine collections to shine a spotlight on well-curated cellars. This approach is resulting in immense bidding interest and clearance rates exceeding 80%, ultimately leading to higher market prices.

“Wine is now a serious alternative asset class, much like watches and art. Values have surged 10 to 20 times in just the past ten years. Take Domaine de la Romanee Conti Marey Monge, Romanee-St-Vivant which has routinely sold for around $600 20 years ago and is now fetching $5,000. It’s hard to imagine that momentum stopping,” Anderson continued.

But while the shift is evident, the storytelling and passion behind fine collection is definitely not lost, according to Anderson.

“Australian wine collectors look to international wines to travel the world through their cellars, with every bottle a time capsule offering a direct, sensory connection to a producer, time and place. A purchase of a fine international wine is securing a unique and rare piece of cultural capital.

“There is a profound connection forged when we share rare bottles. By placing a hard-to-find icon before fellow connoisseurs, we signal a shared appreciation for the history behind the label and create truly memorable experiences.”

 

‘France: the “defensive anchor” for fine wine investment’

The three historic French pillars of Burgundy (57 wines), Bordeaux (37 wines) and Champagne (14 wines) craft the architecture of the classification, “offering an unmatched combination of institutional trust, prestige and financial predictability”. Key French wines in the classification include: Krug Vintage Champagne, Domaine de la Romanee Conti Romanee Conti, Le Pin Pomerol, JL Chave Hermitage and Dagueneau Silex.

“This classification further cements France as the defensive anchor for investment portfolios. Burgundy supplies that scarcity and value appreciation, while Bordeaux holds liquidity and institutional trust for investors.”

 

‘Italy: a market arbitrage for savvy investors’

Across Italy’s 17 entries, Tuscany and Piedmont make up the majority with eight and seven wines respectively. But as a whole, Italian wines, particularly Piedmontese Nebbiolo, are “gaining traction globally but not in Australia, presenting investors an opportunity to invest ahead of the curve”.

“We are currently seeing a unique arbitrage opportunity in Australia: as global demand for Nebbiolo surges, the local market’s lag allows savvy investors to secure elite assets before that momentum catches up. Furthermore, Veneto’s Quintarelli provides a unique anchor for our Italian selection, operating in a vacuum of prestige that is untouched by standard market cycles,” explained Anderson.

 

‘New Zealand’

New Zealand’s nine entries hail from regions Central Otago, Martinborough, Northern Canterbury and Hawke’s Bay. Central Otago’s Felton Road led the charge with four entries including the Block 5 Pinot Noir; Block 3 Pinot Noir; Cornish Point Pinot Noir and the Block 2 Chardonnay. However, its Martinborough that Anderson noted:

“Martinborough’s presence on the international stage is secured by three benchmark producers: Ata Rangi, Kusuda, and Dry River. These wines have earned trust in the secondary market because they consistently bypass commercial trend cycles, trading entirely on pedigree and ultra-low production volumes.”

 

‘Other countries’

Cabernet Sauvignon from the Napa Valley in the US makes a strong appearance with examples from Dominus Estate, Chateau Montelena, Cardinale, Colgin Cariad and Opus One. German Riesling also makes its mark with three entries from iconic producers Dr Loosen, Joh. Jos. Prüm and Keller with their iconic G-Max. Spain and Portugal round out the list with two entries each including historic Vintage Ports from Taylors and Warres plus rare bottlings from Vega Sicilia Único and Marqués de Murrieta Castillo Ygay.

“For those investors looking for diversification of their portfolios beyond France, the wines included in the Classification of International Wine from US, Germany, Spain and Portugal provide trustworthy and reliable options. Their relevance is ever-enduring, take Tenuta Dellórnellaia Masseto for example, a wine that has more than doubled in value under the hammer in less than a decade,” he said.

The Classification of International Wine has been developed through secondary market auction data collected over the last five years from every international bottle that has been traded through Langtons. Unlike its Australian counterpart, the Classification of International Wine does not feature a ‘First Classified’ and ‘Classified’ section, with the entire list referred to as ‘First Classified’.

content:
Young Viticulturist and Winemaker of the Year finalists are gearing up to “battle it out” at the national finals in Martinborough this month.

Five finalists will compete in the 2026 Ormond Nurseries Young Viticulturist of the Year competition at Escarpment on Wednesday 26 August. The competitors include Heath Miller from Pask, Hawke’s Bay; Alex Coombs, Craggy Range, Wairarapa; Kris Godsall, Cloudy Bay, Marlborough; Joshua Irving, Lincoln University, North Canterbury; and Braxton Benseman, Mt. Difficulty, Central Otago.

The 2026 Tonnellerie de Mercurey Young Winemaker of the Year national finalists will compete at Foley’s The Runholder on Tuesday 25 August. The three competitors are Aaron Coxhead, Coxhead Wines, Waikato; Nick Lamain, Isabel Estate, Marlborough; and Joshua Irving, Lincoln University, North Canterbury, the first person ever to compete in both national finals in the same year.

The final challenge for all the competitors will be to deliver their speeches at the New Zealand Wine 2026 Wine Business Forum and Celebration Dinner on 27 August. The winners will be announced that same evening at the Celebration Dinner.

The build-up to the competitions began in January with information sessions and “some very focused contestants signing up prior to vintage”. Regional competitions then took place from May to July.

New Zealand Winegrowers said the commitment from the contestants to grow themselves and the support given by wine industry members as well as sponsors highlights the passion and drive within the wine industry.

“It’s been a huge team effort supporting our future leaders and the positive community spirit around these programmes is very special,” said Nicky Grandorge, leadership & communities manager at New Zealand Winegrowers.

“Everyone involved should be very proud of this.”

In addition to cash prizes, the young viticulturist prize pool includes the Ecotrellis Travel Grant, BioStart Hortisports and Syngenta Biologicals Nutrition prizes, a ‘Leadership Week’, artwork and associate judge at the National Wine Awards.

The young winemakers’ prize pool includes cash, a trip to the Tonnellerie de Mercurey cooperage in Burgundy, Constellation Brands Laboratory and Indevin Wine Judging prizes, an associate judge role at the New World Wine Show, artwork and reviewing wines for DrinksBiz magazine.

Both national winners will receive tickets to Sauvignon Blanc New Zealand 2027 and the Organic Winegrowers Conference.

title: SA government signs agreement with ‘US equivalent of Dan Murphy’s’
summary:
The South Australian government has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with America’s largest wine and liquor retailer Total Wine & More. Described as the US equivalent of Dan Murphy’s, Total Wine & More operates 294 superstores across 30 states and is already one of the largest retail stockists of premium Australian wine in the United States. The agreement, signed by Premier Peter Malinauskas and Total Wine & More chief executive Ryan Ross in Maryland, aims to “deliver closer collaboration between South Australia and Total Wine & More to grow the presence of premium South Australian wines across the retailer’s national network through joint promotions, trade education, buyer engagement and category development over the next 12 to 18 months”.

The post SA government signs agreement with ‘US equivalent of Dan Murphy’s’ appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The South Australian government has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with America’s largest wine and liquor retailer Total Wine & More.

Described as the US equivalent of Dan Murphy’s, Total Wine & More operates 294 superstores across 30 states and is already one of the largest retail stockists of premium Australian wine in the United States.

The agreement, signed by Premier Peter Malinauskas and Total Wine & More chief executive Ryan Ross in Maryland, aims to “deliver closer collaboration between South Australia and Total Wine & More to grow the presence of premium South Australian wines across the retailer’s national network through joint promotions, trade education, buyer engagement and category development over the next 12 to 18 months”.

“South Australia produces some of the finest wine in the world and we’re helping to open more doors so more people around the world can enjoy it,” said Malinauskas.

“At a time when the Australian wine industry is doing it tough, it’s now more important than ever to ensure we’re increasing market share in big overseas markets.”

The state government said the signing builds on an “already strong relationship” and “represents another practical step” to create new export opportunities for SA businesses.

“We have a clear aim to grow our state’s export markets. That means getting in front of major retailers, building long-term partnerships and backing South Australian businesses to compete on the world stage.

“South Australia’s wine industry has an outstanding story to tell. This agreement helps ensure that story reaches more American consumers than ever before,” the Premier said.

The United States remains one of South Australia’s most important wine export markets and is worth more than $130 million per year.

The partnership is said to also allow for senior Total Wine & More executives to visit South Australia for the 2027 International Masters of Wine Symposium in Adelaide and meet directly with producers from across the state’s wine regions.

title: Best’s Great Western invites public to share wine memories for 160th anniversary
summary:
Best’s Great Western is celebrating its 160th anniversary this year, marking the milestone with its “160 Years Poured In” campaign which invites wine lovers to share their own Best’s memories online or at the cellar door. The winery has some of the oldest pre-phylloxera vines in the world, but it shared that it’s the people and their memories which have made the Thomson family the proudest. “Best's wine is poured into 160 years of Australian life - into celebrations, farewells, first dinners, long lunches, quiet evenings. Every bottle that has ever left Great Western has been poured into a moment that mattered to someone. We’d love to hear what some of these were for nostalgic reasons. The stories shared so far, from the trade, wine lovers, and local community have been humbling and so amazing,” said Ben Thomson, managing director and fifth generation family member.

content:
A photo from 1925 featuring Fred H Thomson. Images supplied

Best’s Great Western is celebrating its 160th anniversary this year, marking the milestone with its “160 Years Poured In” campaign which invites wine lovers to share their own Best’s memories online or at the cellar door.

The winery has some of the oldest pre-phylloxera vines in the world, but it shared that it’s the people and their memories which have made the Thomson family the proudest.

“Best’s wine is poured into 160 years of Australian life – into celebrations, farewells, first dinners, long lunches, quiet evenings. Every bottle that has ever left Great Western has been poured into a moment that mattered to someone. We’d love to hear what some of these were for nostalgic reasons. The stories shared so far, from the trade, wine lovers, and local community have been humbling and so amazing,” said Ben Thomson, managing director and fifth generation family member.

The winery’s own history began in 1866, when Henry Best “first recognised the potential of the Great Western region for making wine”. The vines he planted by hand in 1868 are still producing today, among the oldest in the world.

In 1920, the Thomson family became custodians of Best’s, a family that had already established their own winery in Great Western back in 1893.

Ben Thomson is also shortlisted for the ‘2027 Halliday Viticulturist of the Year’ in part for his role in trialling new technology, including UVC light trials and autonomous vehicles in their Great Western vineyards.

“We’ve never been afraid to take risks or try new things, and it’s served us well, through good times and the tougher years. You have to make wine from the heart to continue for five generations. We are committed to remaining customer focused, innovative and ensuring our brand thrives for many years to come,” added Thomson.

Members of the public and the wine trade are invited to share their own Best’s story here or in-person at the cellar door.

content:
Fragos has joined the team at Haselgrove as CEO and chief winemaker. Image supplied

Chairman of McLaren Vale-based winery Haselgrove, Don Totino, has today announced the appointment of esteemed winemaker Michael Fragos to the role of CEO and chief winemaker.

The appointment comes after it was announced last month by Endeavour Group that Fragos had departed from his long-term position at Chapel Hill, where he worked in winemaking roles for 22 years.

Haselgrove said Fragos needs no introduction to the McLaren Vale community, growing up on a local vineyard and having worked 37 vintages “crafting some of the region’s most celebrated wines”.

“I am incredibly proud to have been entrusted by Haselgrove to lead this wonderful winery. It is a privilege to have the opportunity to help shape all aspects of the business. Leading wineries has always been my passion, and Haselgrove offers a truly unique opportunity with its exceptional vineyard, well-equipped winery, and rooftop cellar door,” Fragos shared.

Fragos first worked with now co-owners of Haselgrove, Steve Maglieri, Don Luca and Tony Carrocci at Tatachilla winery in the 1990s. During this time, he also worked as an advisor to fellow co-owner, Don Totino, as he established his Adelaide Hills vineyard. As Fragos moved on from Tatachilla to Chapel Hill Wines, the relationship turned to that of winemaker and grower.

The timing of this next phase was described by Totino as “almost blessed”.

“When (previous CEO) Christophe Forel, decided to make a move to a new industry, at the same time as Michael becoming available, you could say the timing was almost blessed. We didn’t hesitate to bring Michael in. We have absolute trust in his expertise and professionalism; he’s going to take Haselgrove to the next level,” Totino said.

Fragos said he is delighted to continue his connection with the “remarkable” McLaren Vale wine region.

“McLaren Vale is special for so many reasons. It is home to outstanding vineyard sites, breathtaking natural beauty, a pristine coastline and a world-class wine and food culture.

“Above all, it is the people who make this region extraordinary. There is a genuine sense of community, and together we share the privilege and responsibility of being custodians of this beautiful place,” he said.

Fragos is also looking forward to working with long-term senior winemaker Andrew Locke in this new role.

“I am looking forward to working with Andrew and the talented Haselgrove team to continue nurturing and developing this important McLaren Vale winery. Together, we will build on its strong foundations to showcase the character and splendour of this exceptional region through our wines.”

Outside of winemaking, Fragos acts as chair of the McLaren Vale Districts Working Group.

Entries have opened for the 10th annual James Halliday Grenache Challenge.

The challenge is an annual search for the top Grenache from across Australia and was founded in 2017 under the auspices of James Halliday AM.

Judged concurrently with the MGA Insurance Group McLaren Vale Wine Show, the James Halliday Grenache Challenge is open to single-variety Grenache wines from any producer and all wine regions across Australia.

The challenge annually “analyses the diversity of Grenache expressions and winemaking through a competitive tasting to celebrate and elevate the variety, while recognising the effort and excellence of the producers driving the success of Australian Grenache”.

The challenge welcomes wines from emerging winemakers and established wineries that “demonstrate the authenticity, character and exceptional quality of Australian Grenache wines”.

title: Wine Tasmania’s National Wine Trade Visit set for October
summary:
Wine Tasmania’s National Wine Trade Visit is heading to the island’s north from Sunday 11 to Tuesday 13 October 2026, offering 10 selected buyers, sommeliers, retailers and hospitality professionals “a two-day immersion into Tasmania’s wine, people and place”. The event will feature wines from across the island and allow guests to meet growers and makers behind the bottles, taste a range of wine varieties and styles, as well as gain insight into the “conditions, decisions and occasional weather-related chaos which shape the island’s cool climate wines”. Wine Tasmania CEO Sheralee Davies said the visitation program allows mainland wine trade to personally experience and understand the diversity of Tasmanian wine and its viticultural landscape.

The post Wine Tasmania’s National Wine Trade Visit set for October appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Wine Tasmania’s National Wine Trade Visit is heading to the island’s north from Sunday 11 to Tuesday 13 October 2026, offering 10 selected buyers, sommeliers, retailers and hospitality professionals “a two-day immersion into Tasmania’s wine, people and place”.

The event will feature wines from across the island and allow guests to meet growers and makers behind the bottles, taste a range of wine varieties and styles, as well as gain insight into the “conditions, decisions and occasional weather-related chaos which shape the island’s cool climate wines”.

Wine Tasmania CEO Sheralee Davies said the visitation program allows mainland wine trade to personally experience and understand the diversity of Tasmanian wine and its viticultural landscape.

“The best way to discover and appreciate a wine is by visiting the vineyard in which it was grown, kicking the dirt, feeling the (often brisk and always refreshing) air, chatting about the season and talking directly with the people who grew the grapes and made the wine,” Davies said.

“Tasmania’s wine is shaped by its microclimates, landscapes, ever-changing seasons and its hardworking, good-humoured growers and makers. This visit brings all of that together and gives guests an in-depth and deeper understanding of what makes the island’s wines so distinctive and diverse.”

Wine Tasmania said the state produces just 0.9 per cent of Australia’s wine but contributes around five per cent of its farmgate value – “small in volume, rather loud in reputation”.

The organisation added that many of the island’s wines are produced in limited quantities, “making strong relationships between wine producers and key wine trade buyers particularly important”.

“We’re looking for people who are genuinely curious about Tasmanian wine and excited to take what they learn back to their customers, venues and networks,” Davies said.

The October program follows Wine Tasmania’s southern-based National Wine Trade Visit held in May and “forms part of its ongoing work to connect Tasmania’s wine producers with influential wine trade professionals across Australia”.

With only 10 places available, applications are open to mainland-based wine buyers, sommeliers, retailers, distributors and hospitality professionals who directly influence wine purchasing decisions.

content:
Entries are now open and will close Monday 24 August. Image supplied

Entries for the 2026 James Halliday Australian Chardonnay & Cabernet Challenge (JHCACC) have officially opened.

Wineries from across the country are invited to submit their top expressions of these two varieties for the chance to be named the best of their region or even the top wine nationally.

Entries close Monday 24 August with judging taking place at the RACV Healesville Country Club and Resort in the Yarra Valley between September 29 and 30. Results will be announced Tuesday 13 October.

“Wine Yarra Valley and Margaret River Wine are excited to announce that entries are open once again for the James Halliday Australian Chardonnay & Cabernet Challenge and can’t wait to see the outstanding quality of wines submitted for judging,” said committee chair Sarah Crowe.

“The challenge is a fantastic opportunity for Australian wineries to present their best Chardonnay and Cabernet and receive invaluable feedback from a respected panel of industry judges while also being benchmarked among regional peers.”

Entered wineries will have the opportunity to take out the top titles of ‘2026 James Halliday Australian Chardonnay Challenge Winner’ and ‘Cabernet Challenge Winner’. There will also be trophies for ‘Best of Region’ awarded to the highest scoring wine from each featured region, alongside individual gold, silver and bronze medals based on the 100-point system.

New to the challenge for 2026 is the ‘Wine of Provenance Award’, recognising “consistency and quality across multiple vintages of the same wine”. Entry requires a set of three vintages of the same label, covering a minimum spread of eight vintages with a minimum three year spread between them.

“The introduction of the Wine of Provenance Award provides wineries the opportunity to showcase their wines across a series of vintages to highlight consistency and winemaking skill across growing conditions. It also recognises the dedication of our Australian winemakers to their craft and regional expression,” added Crowe.

Last year’s challenge saw the Shaw + Smith Lenswood Vineyard 2023 Chardonnay (Adelaide Hills) take out the title of ‘Chardonnay Challenge Winner’ while the Devils Lair 2023 Margaret River Cabernet Sauvignon was named ‘Cabernet Challenge Winner’.

“Chardonnay has become such an important wine to us both in Australia and around the world, winning the JHCACC has shone a light on the work we are doing and the wines we are making among an amazing field of other producers,” said Adam Wadewitz, Winemaker of Shaw + Smith.

The James Halliday Australian Chardonnay & Cabernet Challenge officially launched in 2021 after operating as separate award programs in the Yarra Valley, Margaret River and Coonawarra respectively. The challenge now operates as a joint endeavour between Margaret River Wine Association and Wine Yarra Valley, with the regions hosting the challenge in alternating years.

content:
The event hasn’t been hosted in Sydney for 15 years. Image supplied

15 years since it was last hosted in Sydney, founding Margaret River winery Cape Mentelle is bringing its International Cabernet Tasting back to the east coast on Friday 16 October.

The event will be held at Watersedge at Campbell’s Stores with views of Sydney Harbour. Organisers said the tasting will feature a lineup of “some of the world’s finest Cabernet labels”.

Tickets for the event are now on sale on the Cape Mentelle website for $750 per person. Tickets include a blind tasting across three brackets of local and global Cabernet with commentary from key Australian wine media before all is revealed at the end.

The tasting is then followed by a Champagne palate cleanser, before guests sit down for a long lunch “expertly paired with the wines from the tasting”.

“I’m excited to bring this much-loved wine tasting experience back to Sydney for the first time since 2011,” said Cape Mentelle chief of winemaking and viticulture David Moulton.

“Each year, the tasting reveals the ever-evolving landscape of cabernet sauvignon, as seen through the lens of some of the world’s best winemakers. Not only do we see how our own Cabernet is looking against an array of other Australian releases, but we get to see how Margaret River Cabernet continues to define itself against regions from around the world. I can’t wait to see what the tasting unveils.”

While the exact lineup for 2026 remains a secret until the final reveal on the day, organisers said guests can anticipate “an exceptional showcase of benchmark Cabernet Sauvignon”. The tasting will feature “iconic Australian expressions alongside cult-status international producers from Italy (including famed Super Tuscans), the US, New Zealand and France”.

This year’s event will offer Australia’s exclusive first look at the acclaimed 2023 Bordeaux vintage prior to its official local arrival. Featuring “stellar” examples from First and Second Growth producers, attendees will enjoy “a preview of a widely applauded vintage destined for strictly limited allocation nationwide”.

The Cape Mentelle International Cabernet Tasting is one of Australia’s longest running international wine benchmark tastings, established in 1982 by Cape Mentelle founder David Hohnen. The tasting initially began as a process to “help Hohnen finesse each vintage by benchmarking his own releases against globally recognised expressions”.

Today, the tasting has expanded to invite wine lovers to join the Cape Mentelle team to taste and benchmark Cabernet from across the world alongside home-grown examples from the same vintage.

content:
The Australian Pinot Noir Challenge has opened entries for the 2026 competition.

Now in its 9th year, the event is “known for its rigorous judging process and esteemed panel of judges” and “recognised as a significant accolade in the wine industry”.

Entries close Tuesday 11 August, with entry delivery between Tuesday 17 August and Friday 28 August. Judging will take place from Tuesday 8 to Wednesday 9 September, with trophy announcement to be advised.

The 2026 judging panel will be chaired by Pinot Noir fanatic Tom Carson and includes Michael Downer, Brendan Hawker, Imogen Dillon, Tillie Johnston, Adam Cotterall and Leanne Altmann, with associates Charlie Warne, Thomas Borghesi, Grace Jiranek and Matthew Lugg.

Carson, chair of judges, said Australian Pinot Noir is among the finest varieties with so much potential still to be unlocked.

“Judging this show is a highlight because it provides a chance to see how viticulturists and winemakers are mastering this notoriously challenging variety. It is in the vineyard where the potential is set, and as the show is judged regionally, it provides an opportunity to showcase what is happening in the region and who the regional stars are. It is a detailed and precise assessment that offers grapegrowers and winemakers a chance to benchmark themselves against their peers.

“In 2025, eight regions were recognised with Regional Trophies, highlighting the remarkable evolution and growing depth of Pinot Noir across Australia. It’s pleasing to see the standard continue to rise, with outstanding wines now emerging from an increasingly diverse range of regions,” Carson said.

The competition aims to highlight the “incredible diversity and quality of Australian Pinot Noir” as well as provide a platform for winemakers to showcase their craftsmanship.

Lindsay McCall, chair of the challenge, said the organisers are incredibly proud of how the challenge has evolved over the past nine years.

“The quality of entries continues to impress us, and it is truly inspiring to see how winning the challenge can transform a winery’s trajectory.”

In 2025, the Yarra Valley broke Tasmania’s five-year streak at the Australian Pinot Noir Challenge. The Yarra Valley took out the top prize with Giant Steps’ 2024 Applejack Vineyard Pinot Noir crowned the 2025 Trophy winner — the first time the region has claimed the honour.

Since taking the helm at Giant Steps in 2021, winemaker Mel Chester has overseen a string of major accolades.

“Applejack is a special site, particularly for Pinot Noir, and is diligently cared for by our vineyard and winery teams. To win the Australian Pinot Noir Challenge for the first time on behalf of the region is a huge honour for our team and for the Yarra Valley,” Chester said.

McCall added that seeing Yarra Valley secure the win last year was a big achievement.

“For the past five years, Tasmania dominated the competition, so to see the Yarra Valley secure its first challenge win last year, bringing the number of winning regions to four over the past nine years, was a significant milestone. It highlights the remarkable strength and diversity of Australian Pinot Noir across multiple regions and the world-class calibre of wines being produced throughout the country.

“We encourage all Pinot Noir producers to enter the 2026 Australian Pinot Noir Challenge and be part of this exciting journey.”
